## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- The sources found do not support this break's listed size range.
- The sources found do not support this break's listed swell period.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the best swell direction.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the best wind direction.

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> 9 sources: 8 read directly, plus SurferToday kept unchanged as web_search (403). 7 publishers. Wind is well supported: Wikipedia (SW monsoon offshore, island-wide), Surf-Forecast (SW best/offshore), Fat Lips (best wind SW) and Strike Mission's profile (SW, 180-270 offshore range). All are 35 deg from the profile's 260, within tolerance, but they centre on 225; consider moving offshore_wind_direction toward 225-240. Swell direction: Surf-Forecast, Fat Lips and Siargao Local say NE (45); Strike Mission's profile says NE 20-90. Every source puts the best direction about 15 deg north of the profile's 60-110 optimum, so consider widening optimal_min to about 45. Size: Fat Lips gives a best range of 2-10 ft, which matches the 10 ft max (the min is 2, not 3). The WSL contest reports (2018, 2024) saw excellent 4-6 ft days. Period: only Strike Mission's 14 s reference (a model input, community) gives a number; the 9/13 s profile values are otherwise unsupported. Tide: Surf-Forecast high and rising, Fat Lips mid-high, Siargao Local mid-to-high, Strike Mission mid-to-high, In Siargao mid. A WSL report saw fewer barrels as the tide dropped. All support mid_to_high. Season: Wikipedia Aug-Dec (island-wide), Fat Lips late Aug-Nov, Siargao Local and In Siargao Aug-Nov, Strike Mission Aug-Nov. These match the profile's Aug-Nov. Surf-Forecast's guide text says autumn and winter, while its raw-HTML season widget says summer/September, an internal inconsistency. Strike Mission calls Aug-Nov the 'NE monsoon', but in the Philippines Aug-Nov is the SW (habagat) monsoon, which points to generated text. Its values are a scoring profile labelled 'community' data. Siargao Local and In Siargao are 2026 web guides of unknown authorship. Fat Lips is a local surf school (undated). No peer-reviewed or Philippine government source about the break was found; Crossref returned only general reef-hydrodynamics and tourism papers. Bathymetry remains unmeasured: the evidence is Wikipedia's Philippine Trench statement and SurferToday (unread).

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Geography

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Break type | reef (right, with a shorter left) | documented | S1, S2, S3, S4 | `break_type` reef, `wave_direction` right |

Notes:

- **Break type**: Wikipedia calls it a right-breaking reef wave, Surf-Forecast an exposed reef break with left and right breaking reefs, SurferToday (search summary) says the right is the main attraction and the left is shorter, and WSL reports lefts and rights in competition.
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “with a reputation for thick, hollow tubes is "Cloud 9". This right-breaking reef wave is the site of the annual Siargao Cup”
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast): “Cloud 9 in Siargao Islands is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf...There are left and right breaking reefs.”
  - S4 (SurferToday): “The right-hander is the main attraction, offering the longest and cleanest barrel sections. The left breaks off the same peak but is shorter, throwing a quick hollow section before shutting down.”
  - S3 (World Surf League): “The lefts were really good in that heat and were staying a bit more open than the rights”
- **Orientation**: Wikipedia says the island's Pacific-facing reefs sit on the edge of the Philippine Trench; it gives no bearing for Cloud 9 itself.
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “The island's Pacific-facing reefs are situated on the edge of the Philippine Trench, and the extremely deep offshore waters assure the ocean swells have undiluted power”
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed reef break.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast): “Cloud 9 in Siargao Islands is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf...There are left and right breaking reefs.”
- **Bathymetry**: SurferToday (search summary) speaks of a shallow coral reef fed by swell funnelled from nearby deep water, and Wikipedia says Siargao's Pacific-facing reefs sit on the edge of the Philippine Trench; no survey is cited.
  - S4 (SurferToday): “a higher tide also helps by adding a little more water over the shallow coral reef, making the wave slightly more forgiving”
  - S4 (SurferToday): “the Pacific swell is funneled in from nearby deep water, which helps create hollow barrels”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “The island's Pacific-facing reefs are situated on the edge of the Philippine Trench, and the extremely deep offshore waters assure the ocean swells have undiluted power”
